title: Regulatory Enabling Basis for Customs Rule-Making
summary: The Third Schedule serves as the primary legislative anchor for the National Board of Revenue (NBR) to issue or amend subordinate legislation under Section 219 of the Customs Act, 1969. Over time, specific items within the Schedule (notably Item 17 for baggage rules, Item 21 for licensing, and Paragraph 8 for general procedures) have been consistently invoked to provide the legal authority for administrative notifications.

evolution.legal_basis: The reliance on specific items within the Third Schedule has shifted from general rule-making authority to targeted item-specific mandates for different regulatory domains (baggage vs. licensing vs. general procedures).
evolution.scope: Expanded from basic licensing and baggage rules to include procedural repeals and specific administrative powers.

timeline.change: Initial invocation of Item 21 for licensing rules and freight forwarder regulations.
Invocation of Item 17 for baggage rule amendments.
Introduction of Paragraph 8 as a specific legal basis for rule-making.
Use of Item 17 to authorize the repeal of obsolete baggage rules.

Third Schedule: Item 21 of this schedule is cited as the regulatory basis for the administrative powers exercised in this notification.
National Board of Revenue: This body exercises its statutory authority to amend existing customs licensing regulations.
Customs Agents (Licensing) Rules 2009: These rules are amended to modify the composition of licensing committees and administrative requirements.
The amendments specify new documentation requirements regarding income tax assessment for applicants.
The penalty structure for activities unrelated to customs duties is revised to set a specific minimum and maximum range.

Customs Act 1969: Sections 207 and 219 of this Act provide the authority for the National Board of Revenue to amend licensing rules, read in conjunction with the Third Schedule.
Freight Forwarders (Licensing and Operat: These rules are subject to several amendments including the update of licensing authority references, deletion of specific form requirements, extension of time-based procedural limits, and modification of documentary requirements for license eligibility.
National Board of Revenue: The Board exercises its regulatory authority under the Customs Act 1969 to revise the operational and licensing framework for freight forwarders.
Customs Agents (Licensing) Rules 2009: This rule set is now the correct reference for the licensing authority constitution replacing references to older 1986 rules within the freight forwarder licensing framework.

Customs Act 1969: This act serves as the primary legal authority for the National Board of Revenue to issue regulatory orders and amend customs rules.
National Board of Revenue: The board is empowered under the Customs Act to amend existing baggage rules to regulate the import of goods by passengers.
Passenger (Non-Tourist) Baggage (Import): These rules are amended to place a frequency limit on the duty-free baggage allowance that a passenger can claim within a calendar year.
The amendments also revise the duty-tax rates for specific television technologies based on screen size and remove certain previously listed entries.
The rules are further updated to define specific television size thresholds for duty-free status and to add a new category for duty-free import of carpets within a defined surface area limit.
Third Schedule: The Third Schedule of the Customs Act is referenced as part of the legal basis for the current regulatory amendments.
Imported Vehicle: While the SRO updates baggage rules, it specifically targets and amends the duty structures and eligibility for electronics and personal goods such as televisions and carpets under the existing passenger baggage framework.
